newsitem.title: THAILAND: More pain seen for Thai stocks before gain.
newsitem.headline: More pain seen for Thai stocks before gain.

text.p: With Thai stocks sharply down this week, the bulls that charged in on an apparent market recovery last week may have moved too soon, analysts said on Tuesday.
A 2.0 percent fall in the Thai share market on Monday, and continued losses on Tuesday, brought investors sharply back to earth after hefty gains last week.
The SET index dropped 2.14 percent in thin trade by the lunch break on Tuesday, shedding 17.60 points to 805.29.
"I think the change in sentiment last week can be attributed to irrational exuberance," Brett Williams, senior vice-president at Krungthai Thanakit Plc, told Reuters.
"A lot of people just couldn't resist these prices and are hoping they haven't mistaken a positive trend," he said.
A host of investor concerns also suggests that the market is set to fall further in the near term, analysts said.

"I think the market will need to consolidate and could test lower levels before recovering," George Morgan, country manager at HG Asia said. Upbeat comments by some global strategists, Thai government plans to trim the budget and the launching of a property sector support package fuelled a near 7.0 percent New Year rise in the market between January 3 and January 10.
Investors had hoped for a sustained rally after the market fell to more than four year lows following a deterioration in the country's economic climate in 1996.

Instead, Monday's slide in the index confirmed suspicions that sentiment remains fickle and the market now appears to be softening ahead of the fourth quarter corporate results expected next month, which are widely forecast to be miserable.
"It seems like the fourth quarter earnings fears may drive down the market," said Nokorn Kolfrichai, executive vice president at Chao Phaya Finance and Securities.
"It could be that everyone is waiting to see the earnings and after that we might see the macro trends getting better. I think this will be the worst month this year for the market," he said.

Although Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's new government won plaudits for trimming the budget and moving to address a bad loan problem brought on by an ailing property sector, analysts said most foreign investors were sidelined until clear signs emerged that the measures had impact.

"The government has indicated a willingness to address the key issues but I don't think we will see a large return of foreign money unless there is some concrete evidence that things are getting better," said HG Asia's Morgan.

Analysts said investors are looking for signs of a pick-up in export growth, a resurgence of economic growth which slowed to 6.7 percent last year, and a reduction in Thailand's current account deficit which stood at 8.2 percent of GDP last year.

The market remains dominated by domestic considerations, but the current account deficit leaves it vulnerable to external shock, and U.S. jobs data released last week renewed worries of a possible rise in U.S. interest rates.

A hike in U.S. rates would almost certainly kill hopes of cuts in Thai domestic rates, analysts said. Thai rates have remained among the highest in the region in order to attract capital to finance the current account deficit.
